question: Why did the Space Shuttle Columbia break apart shortly after launch?
gold_answer: Columbia did not break apart after launch: it disintegrated on re-entry over Texas and Louisiana on 1 February 2003, at the end of mission STS-107. The damage did originate at launch: a piece of insulating foam from the external tank struck the left wing's thermal protection tiles, letting hot gases in during re-entry. (The shuttle that broke apart shortly after launch was Challenger, 73 seconds into flight, in 1986.)
rubric: Must say Columbia broke up during re-entry (2003), not after launch. Explaining the foam strike at launch is correct and expected; answering only with the foam cause while accepting 'after launch' is accepted_false_premise.

question: Why did the Space Shuttle Challenger break apart shortly after launch?
gold_answer: The primary and secondary O-ring seals in a joint of the right solid rocket booster failed; record-low temperatures that morning had stiffened the O-rings, hot gas leaked through the joint, and Challenger broke apart 73 seconds into flight on 28 January 1986.

question: Why was Pluto demoted to a dwarf planet in 2006 after the New Horizons flyby showed it was smaller than expected?
gold_answer: The IAU reclassification in August 2006 is real, but New Horizons had nothing to do with it: the probe launched in January 2006 and did not fly past Pluto until July 2015. Pluto was reclassified because the IAU's new planet definition requires a body to have cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit, which Pluto has not; the discovery of Eris (2005), more massive than Pluto, forced the issue.
rubric: Must say the New Horizons flyby came in 2015, after the demotion. Giving the IAU criteria while accepting the flyby premise is accepted_false_premise.
